'''''Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life''''' (acronymed: SITG) is a 2018 nonfiction book by [[Nassim Nicholas Taleb]], a former [[options (finance)|options]] trader with a background in the mathematics of [[probability]] and [[statistics]].

Taleb's thesis is that [[skin in the game (phrase)|skin in the game]]—i.e., having a shared risk when taking a major decision—is necessary for fairness, commercial efficiency, and risk management, as well as being necessary to understand the world.<ref name=introduction>{{cite book|last1=Taleb|first1=Nassim Nicholas|title=Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life|date=2018|publisher=[[Random House]]|isbn=9780425284629|language=en|chapter=Introduction}}</ref> The book is part of Taleb's multi-volume philosophical essay on uncertainty, titled the ''[[Incerto]]'', which also includes ''[[Fooled by Randomness]]'' (2001), ''[[The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable|The Black Swan]]'' (2007–2010), ''[[The Bed of Procrustes]]'' (2010–2016), and ''[[Antifragile (book)|Antifragile]]'' (2012). The book is dedicated to "two men of courage": [[Ron Paul]], "a Roman among Greeks"; and [[Ralph Nader]], "Greco-Phoenician saint".<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vqZJDwAAQBAJ&q=%22Ralph+Nader%22&pg=PA32|title=Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life|first=Nassim Nicholas|last=Taleb|date=15 April 2018|publisher=Random House|via=Google Books|isbn=9780425284629}}</ref>

==Asymmetry and missing incentives==
If an actor pockets some rewards from a policy they enact or support without accepting any of the risks, economists consider it to be a problem of "missing incentives". In contrast, to Taleb, the problem is more fundamentally one of asymmetry: one actor gets the rewards, the other is stuck with the risks.<ref name=introduction/>

Taleb argues that "For social justice, focus on symmetry and risk sharing. You cannot make profits and transfer the risks to others, as bankers and large corporations do... Forcing [[skin in the game (phrase)|skin in the game]] corrects this asymmetry better than thousands of laws and regulations."<ref name=guardian>{{cite news|last1=Williams|first1=Zoe|title=Skin in the Game by Nassim Nicholas Taleb review – how risk should be shared|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2018/feb/22/skin-in-the-game-nassim-nicholas-taleb-review|access-date=24 February 2018|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=22 February 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref name="ft">{{cite news |last=Gapper |first=John |date=20 February 2018 |title=Should risk-takers be required to have 'skin in the game'? |work=[[Financial Times]] |url=https://www.ft.com/content/704ee604-1561-11e8-9e9c-25c814761640 |access-date=24 February 2018}}</ref><ref name=economist>{{cite news|title=Nassim Taleb explains the power of "skin in the game"|url=https://www.economist.com/news/books-and-arts/21737240-and-settles-some-old-scores-nassim-taleb-explains-power-skin-game|access-date=24 February 2018|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=2018|language=en}}</ref>

=== The centrality of negative incentives ===
Actors – per Taleb – must bear a cost when they fail the public. A [[fund manager]] that gets a percentage on wins, but no penalty for losing, is incentivized to gamble with his clients' funds. Bearing no downside for one's actions means that one has no "skin in the game", which is the source of many evils.

An [[evolutionary process]] is an additional argument for SITG. Those who err and have SITG will not survive; hence, evolutionary processes will eliminate (physically or figuratively by going bankrupt etc.) those tending to do stupid things. Without SITG, this process cannot work.

===Examples===
[[Robert Rubin]], a highly-paid director and senior advisor at [[Citigroup]], paid no financial penalty when Citigroup had to be rescued by U.S. taxpayers due to the [[2008 financial crisis]].<ref name=ft/> Taleb calls this sort of a trade, with upside gain but no or limited downside risk, a "Bob Rubin trade".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mayer |first=Chris |date=23 April 2018 |title=Four Simple Things You Should Do to Succeed In the Stock Market |url=https://www.palmbeachgroup.com/palm-beach-daily/four-simple-things-you-should-do-to-succeed-in-the-stock-market/ |access-date=27 September 2023 |website=Palm Beach Research Group}}</ref>

Many [[war hawk]]s do not themselves bear any risks of dying in a war they advocate.

==Intellectual Yet Idiot==
''Intellectual Yet Idiot'' (IYI) is a term coined by Taleb in his essay by the same name that refers to the semi-intelligent well-pedigreed  "who are telling us 1) what to do, 2) what to eat, 3) how to speak, 4) how to think... and 5) who to vote for". They represent a very small minority of people but have an overwhelming impact on the vast majority because they affect government policy. IYI are often policy makers, academics, journalists, and media pundits.

{{blockquote | The IYI pathologizes others for doing things he doesn't understand without ever realizing it is his understanding that may be limited. He thinks people should act according to their best interests and he knows their interests, particularly if they are "[[red neck]]s" or English non-crisp-vowel class who voted for [[Brexit]]. When plebeians do something that makes sense to them, but not to him, the IYI uses the term "uneducated". What we generally call participation in the political process, he calls by two distinct designations: "democracy" when it fits the IYI, and "populism" when the plebeians dare voting in a way that contradicts his preferences.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://medium.com/@nntaleb/the-intellectual-yet-idiot-13211e2d0577#.3v9bolkbw | title = The Intellectual Yet Idiot, By Nassim Nicholas Taleb| date = 21 January 2018}}</ref>}}

Taleb points out that being educated and "intellectual" does not always mean that someone is not an idiot for most purposes. "You can be an intellectual yet still be an idiot. 'Educated [[Philistinism|philistine]]s' have been wrong on everything from [[Stalinism]] to [[Iraq conflict (2003–present)|Iraq]] to [[low-carbohydrate diet|low-carb diets]]."

Taleb dedicates a chapter to IYIs in the book.

===Usage===
The term was picked up and used late in the 2016 U.S. presidential election by [[Newt Gingrich]] when he criticized the negative response Trump received after the first presidential debate stating that "The Intellectual Yet Idiot class is so out of touch with America that they don't even realize how badly they are doing and how well Trump is doing."<ref>{{cite web |last=Gingrich |first=Newt |date=27 September 2016 |title=Newt Gingrich: Trump won the debate. Don't believe the "Intellectual Yet Idiot" class |url=https://www.foxnews.com/opinion/newt-gingrich-trump-won-the-debate-dont-believe-the-intellectual-yet-idiot-class/ |website=Fox News}}</ref> Gingrich has mentioned the term in interviews and speeches since then<ref>{{cite web |date=24 December 2016 |title=TRUMP ADMINISTRATION POLICY AGENDA, "Intellectual Yet Idiot" |url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?c4640535/intellectual-yet-idiot |access-date=18 July 2017 |website=C-SPAN}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=15 December 2016 |title=Gingrich Predicts Cabinet Will Dismantle Federal Bureaucracy |url=https://www.bna.com/gingrich-predicts-cabinet-n73014448627 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161216155209/https://www.bna.com/gingrich-predicts-cabinet-n73014448627/ |archive-date=16 December 2016 |website=[[Bloomberg BNA]] |quote=About 288,000 federal workers are employed in Washington, and 'I'll guarantee you' 35 percent or 40 percent of them fit Taleb's description. The answer is not to figure out how to manage them, but to get rid of them.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=It's the end of the world as we know it |url=http://www.newsday.com/opinion/oped/it-s-the-end-of-the-world-as-we-know-it-1.12984271 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905160951/http://www.newsday.com/opinion/oped/it-s-the-end-of-the-world-as-we-know-it-1.12984271 |archive-date=5 September 2017 |website=[[Newsday]]}}</ref> and has included in his book ''Understanding Trump'' a chapter called "The Rise of the IYI".<ref>{{cite book |author=Gingrich |first=Newt |title=Understanding Trump |publisher=Center Street |year=2017 |isbn=978-1478923084 |location=New York}}</ref>

The term has since been used extensively and has been cited in numerous periodicals including ''[[The Guardian]]'',<ref>{{cite web |last=Nevins |first=Jake |date=20 June 2017 |title=Understanding Trump: what can we learn from Newt Gingrich's new book? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/jun/20/newt-gingrich-book-understanding-trump |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> ''[[Financial Times]]'',<ref>{{cite web |last=Leith |first=Sam |date=28 February 2018 |title='Brexit Brains' fail to enlighten us |url=https://www.ft.com/content/a21da152-1b01-11e8-a748-5da7d696ccab |website=[[Financial Times]]}}</ref> and ''[[New Statesman]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Poole |first=Steven |date=5 March 2018 |title=Why author Nassim Nicholas Taleb is the ideal public thinker for the age of Trump |url=https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/books/2018/03/why-author-nassim-nicholas-taleb-ideal-public-thinker-age-trump |website=[[New Statesman]]}}</ref> [[Jonah Goldberg]], in an article from ''[[National Review]]'', references the term in defense of non-liberal intellectuals who have been branded "anti-intellectual" by the Left.<ref>{{cite web |last=Goldberg |first=Jonah |date=20 February 2017 |title=The Science of Intellectual Tribalism |url=http://www.nationalreview.com/article/444042/david-gelernter-science-adviser-candidate-subject-lefts-latest-smear-campaign |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170711121126/http://www.nationalreview.com/article/444042/david-gelernter-science-adviser-candidate-subject-lefts-latest-smear-campaign |archive-date=11 July 2017 |website=[[National Review]]}}</ref>
Graham Vyse, in his article "Democrats Should Stop Talking About Bipartisanship and Start Fighting" from ''[[The New Republic]]'', referenced Gingrich's use of IYI as divisive and that until the Republicans become more collaborative, "Democrats need to drop the subject, too, and fight like hell instead."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Vyse |first=Graham |date=15 December 2016 |title=Democrats Should Stop Talking About Bipartisanship and Start Fighting |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/139353/democrats-stop-talking-bipartisanship-start-fighting |magazine=[[The New Republic]]}}</ref>

==Other ideas==

===Minority rules===

A "stubborn minority", accounting for as little as 4% of the population, can impose its will on the relatively uninterested majority. A [[halal]] eater, for example, will never eat non-halal food, but a non-halal eater is not banned from eating halal. Thus, a catering company switches to serving halal meat despite it being preferred only by a tiny minority of its customers. This happens because it is easier to switch to halal entirely than to have separate halal and non-halal options.<ref name=guardian/><ref name=economist/>

Taleb further argues that, for 
[[Genetically modified crops|"transgenic" genetically modified crops]] to succeed commercially, more than 96% of the population would need to be convinced that they are safe. A "stubborn minority", of just 4%, that opposes GMO food is 
large enough to impose its will on the entire population.

Taleb explains that the process of "minority rule" is done incrementally. An example is given in the book: one stubborn daughter (who refuses to eat GMO food), who lives in a family, can cause her entire family to refuse GMO food simply by refusing GMO food herself. The family finds it easier to eat non-GMO food entirely than to cater separately to the daughter; the family effectively becomes entirely non-GMO-consuming. Similarly, because the family is known in the neighborhood to only consume non-GMO food, a local barbeque would serve only non-GMO food, thus influencing the entire neighborhood to only eat non-GMO food. In turn, local stores would only sell non-GMO food. Therefore, one person in a neighborhood can influence everyone through a stubborn choice.

===Christology===
The book delves into [[Christology]]. Michael Bonner writes: "Observers who are interested in, or baffled by, the Christological debates of the first five hundred years of Christianity may be shocked by Taleb's explanation for the Church's insistence upon the full humanity of Jesus. The short answer is that it was essential for God to have—literally—skin in the game, and that Christ's full participation in crucifixion, self-sacrifice, and death made him the archetypal risk-taker."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bonner |first=Michael R. J. |date=Spring–Summer 2018 |title=Aphorisms from Antique Lands |journal=[[The Dorchester Review]]}}</ref>

==Reception and criticism==
Economist [[Branko Milanović]] wrote that Taleb has created "a full system that goes from empirics to ethics, a thing which is exceedingly rare in modern world."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Milanovic |first=Branko |date=29 January 2018 |title=The Importance of Taleb's System: From the Fourth Quadrant to the Skin in the Game |url=https://www.globalpolicyjournal.com/blog/29/01/2018/importance-talebs-system-fourth-quadrant-skin-game |access-date=2023-09-27 |website=Global Policy Journal}}</ref> ''[[The Economist]]'' described reading the book as similar to "being trapped in a cab with a cantankerous and over-opinionated driver."<ref name="economist" />
Matthew Syed of ''[[The Times]]'' was "mostly persuaded" by the main argument of the book.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Syed |first=Matthew |date=27 September 2023 |title=Review: Skin in the Game by Nassim Nicholas Taleb — down with the 'Intellectual Idiots' |work=[[The Times]] |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/review-skin-in-the-game-by-nassim-nicholas-taleb-down-with-the-intellectual-idiots-f2hp5gvd3 |access-date=27 September 2023 |issn=0140-0460}}</ref> ''[[The Guardian]]'' published an ambivalent review, noting that Taleb's "combination of fearlessness, self-belief and immodesty adds up to charisma on the page" but that "every idea that sounds as if it might work in the abstract fails in the particular".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Zoe |date=22 February 2018 |title=Skin in the Game by Nassim Nicholas Taleb review – how risk should be shared |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2018/feb/22/skin-in-the-game-nassim-nicholas-taleb-review |access-date=27 September 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}
</ref> Taleb responded with a list of the flaws and "reading comprehension" in the reviews in ''The Economist'' and ''The Guardian'' (claiming that journalists have an [[agency problem]] with subjects criticizing their profession for lack of skin of the game).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Taleb |first=Nassim Nicholas |date=3 June 2018 |title=Putting Skin in the Game into the Reviewers of Skin in the Game |url=https://medium.com/incerto/the-controversy-around-skin-in-the-game-6d46416ee47f |access-date=27 September 2023 |website=[[INCERTO]]}}</ref>

===Audiobook===
The audiobook version is narrated by [[Joe Ochman]] and reached No. 4 on [[Audible (store)|Audible.com]]'s nonfiction list in March 2018.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 March 2018 |title=The top 10 audiobooks on Audible.com |url=https://wtop.com/entertainment/2018/03/the-top-10-audiobooks-on-audible-com/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181017042943/https://wtop.com/entertainment/2018/03/the-top-10-audiobooks-on-audible-com/ |archive-date=17 October 2018 |website=wtop.com |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref>
